content: Neuraminidase inhibitors (NIs), such as oseltamivir and zanamivir, are widely used for the treatment and prevention of both seasonal and pandemic influenza. These drugs are stockpiled and recommended by public health agencies globally. However, their clinical efficacy and safety profiles have been the subject of extensive investigation and debate. Time to Symptom Alleviation In adults, oseltamivir reduced the time to the first alleviation of influenza symptoms by an average of 16.8 hours, shortening the duration of symptoms from 7 days to 6.3 days. This effect was statistically significant (P < 0.0001). However, no significant benefit was observed in asthmatic children. In otherwise healthy children, oseltamivir reduced symptom duration by an average of 29 hours (P = 0.001). Zanamivir reduced the time to symptom alleviation in adults by 0.6 days, decreasing the mean duration of symptoms from 6.6 days to 6.0 days (P < 0.00001). However, this effect was not significant in children. Subgroup analysis showed no difference in the effect of zanamivir between influenza-infected and non-influenza-infected adults. Hospitalizations Oseltamivir did not significantly reduce the risk of hospitalization in adults, children, or in prophylactic use. The risk difference (RD) was 0.15% (95% CI -0.78 to 0.91). Data on hospitalizations for zanamivir were not reported. Serious Influenza Complications Oseltamivir did not significantly reduce serious complications of influenza or those leading to study withdrawal in adults (RD 0.07%, 95% CI -0.78 to 0.44) or children. Similarly, zanamivir showed no significant effect on serious complications in adults or in prophylaxis. There were insufficient data to assess these outcomes in children treated with zanamivir or in prophylactic use of oseltamivir. Pneumonia Oseltamivir significantly reduced the risk of self-reported, investigator-mediated, unverified pneumonia in adults (RD 1.00%, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.49; number needed to treat to benefit [NNTB] = 100). However, this effect was not significant in trials that used more detailed diagnostic criteria for pneumonia. No trials reported effects on radiologically confirmed pneumonia. In children, oseltamivir had no significant effect on pneumonia. Zanamivir did not significantly reduce the risk of either self-reported or radiologically confirmed pneumonia in adults or children. In prophylaxis, zanamivir reduced the risk of self-reported, unverified pneumonia in adults (RD 0.32%, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.41; NNTB = 311), but oseltamivir did not. Bronchitis, Sinusitis, and Otitis Media Zanamivir significantly reduced the risk of bronchitis in adults (RD 1.80%, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.80; NNTB = 56). Oseltamivir did not show a significant effect on bronchitis. Neither oseltamivir nor zanamivir significantly reduced the risk of sinusitis or otitis media in adults or children. Adverse Effects of Treatment In adults, oseltamivir increased the risk of nausea (RD 3.66%, 95% CI 0.90 to 7.39; number needed to treat to harm [NNTH] = 28) and vomiting (RD 4.56%, 95% CI 2.39 to 7.58; NNTH = 22). It also decreased the risk of diarrhea (RD 2.33%, 95% CI 0.14 to 3.81; NNTB = 43) and cardiac events (RD 0.68%, 95% CI 0.04 to 1.0; NNTB = 148). Psychiatric adverse events were observed in a dose-dependent manner in two pivotal trials (P = 0.038). In children, oseltamivir increased the risk of vomiting (RD 5.34%, 95% CI 1.75 to 10.29; NNTH = 19). It also reduced the proportion of children with a four-fold increase in antibody titers (relative risk [RR] 0.90, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.00). Zanamivir had a lower toxicity profile compared to oseltamivir, likely due to its lower bioavailability. Prophylaxis Both oseltamivir and zanamivir reduced the risk of symptomatic influenza in individuals (oseltamivir: RD 3.05%, 95% CI 1.83 to 3.88; NNTB = 33; zanamivir: RD 1.98%, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.54; NNTB = 51) and in households (oseltamivir: RD 13.6%, 95% CI 9.52 to 15.47; NNTB = 7; zanamivir: RD 14.84%, 95% CI 12.18 to 16.55; NNTB = 7). Neither drug had a significant effect on asymptomatic influenza. Oseltamivir increased the risk of psychiatric adverse events during prophylaxis (RD 1.06%, 95% CI 0.07 to 2.76; NNTH = 94) and also increased the risk of headaches (RD 3.15%, 95% CI 0.88 to 5.78; NNTH = 32), renal events (RD 0.67%, 95% CI -2.93 to 0.01; NNTH = 150), and nausea (RD 4.15%, 95% CI 0.86 to 9.51; NNTH = 25). Conclusions Oseltamivir and zanamivir have modest effects in reducing the duration of influenza symptoms in adults but not in asthmatic children. Both drugs are effective in reducing the risk of symptomatic influenza when used as prophylaxis. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether these drugs reduce complications of influenza, such as pneumonia, due to a lack of standardized diagnostic criteria. Oseltamivir is associated with an increased risk of adverse effects, including nausea, vomiting, psychiatric events, and renal events in adults, and vomiting in children. Zanamivir has a lower toxicity profile, likely due to its lower systemic absorption. The clinical evidence does not fully support the proposed influenza virus-specific mechanism of action for these drugs. The balance between benefits and harms should be carefully considered when deciding on their use for either treatment or prophylaxis of influenza.
